questions.knowledge_point: Finding Unions and Intersections of Finite Families of Indexed Sets
questions.worked_solution:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for at least one }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Therefore, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i} & ={X}_{-2}\cup {X}_{1}\cup {X}_{2} \\  & ={-2,-1,0}\,\cup \,{0,1}\,\cup \,{0,1,2} \\  & ={-2,-1,0,1,2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Unions and Intersections of (Countably) Infinite Families of Indexed Sets
questions.worked_solution:
The intersection of a family of indexed sets ${{A}_{i}}_{i\in I}$ contains all elements that belong to *all* sets in our family:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for all }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=-1,$ we have ${X}_{-1}={-2,-1}$

- if $i=0,$ we have ${X}_{0}={-1,0}$

- if $i=1,$ we have ${X}_{1}={0,1}$

and so on. 

Notice that there is no element that belongs to all the sets. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}=∅.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Unions and Intersections of (Countably) Infinite Families of Indexed Sets
questions.worked_solution:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for at least one }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

The notation ${⋃}_{i=3}^{\infty }$ means that our set of indexes is 
${3,4,5…}.$ 

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=3,$ we have ${S}_{3}=[\frac{1}{3},1]$

- if $i=4,$ we have ${S}_{4}=[\frac{1}{4},1]$

- if $i=5,$ we have ${S}_{5}=[\frac{1}{5},1]$

- $⋯$

and so on. 

Notice that as $i$ increases, 

- the left endpoint of the intervals approaches $0$ but never reaches it, and

- the right endpoint of the intervals equals $1$ for all the sets.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i=3}^{\infty }{S}_{i}=(0,1].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find $\,\displaystyle \bigcup_{i \in I} S_i$, given that $I = \{ -1, 0, 1 \},$ and $S_i = (i-1, \,i+1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for at least one } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Therefore, in our case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i} & ={S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1} \\  & =(-2,0)\,\cup \,(-1,1)\,\cup \,(0,2) \\  & =(-2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find $\,\displaystyle \bigcap_{i \in I} X_i$  given that $I = \mathbb{N}$ and $X_i = \{ i, \, 2i \}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The intersection of a family of indexed sets $\{A_i\}_{i\in I}$ contains all elements that belong to *all* sets in our family:

$$
\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for all } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=1,$ we have $X_1 = \{ 1, 2 \}$

- if $i=2,$ we have $X_2 = \{ 2, 4 \}$

- if $i=3,$ we have $X_3 = \{ 3, 6 \}$

- if $i=4,$ we have $X_4 = \{ 4, 8 \}$

and so on. 

Notice that there is no element that belongs to all the sets. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}=∅.\end{aligned}
$$
